standard.title: Enlargement Transformation
standard.description: apply the enlargement transformation to shapes and objects using dynamic geometry software as appropriate; identify and explain aspects that remain the same and those that change
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can design, create and test algorithms that identify congruency or similarity of shapes (AC9M8SP04). They have not yet applied the enlargement transformation systematically, or generalised the relationships between scale factor and changes to length, area and volume.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students apply the enlargement transformation to shapes and objects and explain which properties are invariant and which change, including the relationships between scale factor, length, area and volume.

nodes.label: Invariant and changing properties under enlargement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify which properties of a shape are preserved under enlargement (angles, shape) and which change (side lengths, perimeter, area).
nodes.minimum_width: Apply one enlargement transformation to a polygon using a given scale factor; list two properties that remain the same and two that change.
nodes.typical_width: Apply enlargement transformations to a range of 2D shapes with various scale factors (including <1 for reduction); identify invariant properties (angles, shape, orientation) and changing properties (lengths, perimeter, area); verify using measurement and ratio.
wider: Investigate how scale drawings and map scales use enlargement transformations — relate scale factor to real-world dimensions
Explore digital zoom and image resizing — discuss how uniform and non-uniform scaling relate to enlargement and distortion
Connect enlargement to the conditions for similarity established in AC9M8SP01 — confirm that enlargement always produces similar shapes
success_criteria: Correctly applies enlargement transformation and identifies the image dimensions
Lists at least two properties that are invariant (angles, shape) and two that change (lengths, area)
Uses the scale factor correctly to calculate new dimensions

nodes.label: Scale factor relationships for length, area and volume
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can generalise the relationships between scale factor k and the scaling of length (×k), area (×k²) and volume (×k³).
nodes.minimum_width: Calculate the area of a shape and its image after enlargement by scale factor k for at least two values of k; identify that area scales by k².
nodes.typical_width: Investigate and generalise the relationships: lengths scale by k, areas scale by k², volumes scale by k³; verify using numerical examples for whole and rational scale factors; explain why the exponent increases for each dimension.
wider: Investigate biological scaling — why animals of different sizes have proportionally different limb thicknesses (surface area grows as k², volume as k³, requiring thicker bones)
Explore how the k² area relationship applies to similar figures beyond squares and cubes (e.g. similar triangles, similar irregular polygons)
Investigate how the k³ volume relationship applies to 3D objects (e.g. scale models of buildings or aircraft) and what this means for material use

response_modes.reason: Students consistently apply k rather than k² when asked about areas of enlarged figures (and k rather than k³ for volumes). The misconception is resistant because k feels intuitively correct. Multiple examples across different shapes and scale factors — verifying k² each time — is more effective than re-explaining the rule.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The k, k², k³ scaling relationships are a genuinely elegant mathematical result with surprising real-world implications — from biological scaling to packaging design to architectural modelling. Students who explore these connections develop both mathematical insight and cross-disciplinary appreciation.
success_criteria: States and applies the correct scaling relationships: lengths ×k, areas ×k², volumes ×k³
Verifies the area scaling relationship (×k²) for at least two different scale factors
Explains in their own words why area scales as k² (two dimensions each scaled by k)
nodes.hinge_reason: Applying k rather than k² for area (and k rather than k³ for volume) is a near-universal error. Students who carry it cannot correctly solve any problem in AC9M9M03 or AC9M9SP03 that involves scaled areas or volumes.
